title: Inferring Struggle, Judging Strength: How Inferred Adversity and Sympathy Shape Competence Evaluations of Black Frontline Employees
abstract: How do racial inferences shape third-party evaluations of employee competence? Across four experiments, White U.S. observers judged Black frontline employees as more competent than otherwise comparable White employees in service-failure encounters involving a Black customer. This pattern was consistent with a serial process in which employee race cued greater inferred adversity, which elicited sympathy, thereby elevating competence judgments. Study 1 established the competence difference and its association with lower negative word of mouth. Study 2 showed that behavioral awkwardness attenuated the difference. Study 3 supported the serial indirect pathway, and the supplementary pilot reproduced it without a service failure. Study 4 showed that structural-opportunity information increased inferred adversity for both employees and especially increased sympathy and competence judgments for the White employee, narrowing Black–White differences. The findings identify a context-dependent, normatively complex route through which presumed adversity can produce comparatively favorable yet racialized competence judgments.
